title: Fierce 5 novice program review (from an hypertrophy standpoint)
summary: Critiques the Fierce 5 novice program (bodybuilding.com) from a hypertrophy angle. He praises its every-other-day frequency, short sessions, compound focus and acceptance of monotony, but criticises pairing squat and bench on the same day, Pendlay rows and front squats for novices, no pull from the floor, no pull-ups, too little volume from rigid 3x5s, missing arm/hamstring/lower back isolation, and a linear progression that drives you into a plateau. He offers a modified version with rep ranges, deadlifts, push-ups, pull-ups and supersets.

claims.claim: Fierce 5 is a two-workout (A/B) novice program from bodybuilding.com, run one day on, one day off.
Having beginners train every other day is smart for recovery; 3-4 one-hour sessions a week suits novices, who lack the mental stamina for hours in the gym daily.
A novice program built on compound movements is a good sign; one full of machines and cables is a bad program.
Machines and cables are for advanced lifters who know what they're doing; novices find them attractive because they're guided but should 'jump in the sea and swim' with free-weight compounds.

He dislikes doing upper and lower body compounds in the same session because the second compound suffers; he prefers one heavy compound to open the workout followed by variations for the same half of the body.
Squat and bench don't share muscles but they share CNS and stamina demand, so a novice's bench may lag after squatting without them understanding why.
He strongly dislikes novice programs that have you bench and deadlift on the same day, calling it counterproductive.
Pendlay rows are the most technical row variation; especially with a wide grip they need lower back rigidity, hip positioning and hamstring mobility most novices lack.
Horizontal rows, especially from the floor, are not critical for novices; cable rows are preferable until the lifter can row with the back, then move to Pendlay rows.
Novices doing Pendlay rows cheat: no upper back tightness, pull with the arms, no scapular retraction, teaching bad habits.
A novice program without a full-range pull from the floor is a deal breaker; it can be conventional, sumo, Jefferson, trap bar deadlift or Atlas stones, as long as it trains a full hip hinge.

Romanian deadlifts teach good deadlift mechanics, but novices googling them find stiff-legged versions on YouTube, learn the wrong knee flexion and hip travel, and then pull from the floor with stiff legs.
Face pulls are great for beginners and not taxing, so they can be superset with something else.
Calves are not important for novices; they can catch up later, so he doesn't prioritise calf raises in beginner programs.
Tricep pressdowns train the lateral and medial heads but not the long head; skull crushers are not equivalent and should replace pressdowns for novices.
Beginners doing tricep pressdowns tend to engage a lot of shoulder.

He loves front squats but they aren't accessible to novices: they require thoracic extension and spinal mobility novices don't have, leading either to bad form and wrist pain or to wasted energy learning the lift.
Novice programs should use paused back squats instead of front squats; front squats can come later if wanted (e.g. for Olympic lifting).
For most people he does not recommend front squats.
Novices build neural associations quickly, so pairing front squats with overhead press back-to-back risks confusing the two different front rack positions.
Workout B would be better as deadlift, then back squat, then overhead press.
Any novice who can do three or more pull-ups should do pull-ups instead of lat pulldowns; pulldowns are an accessory, not a main lift.
Pull-ups and chin-ups are non-negotiable: they don't tax the CNS, decompress the spine and teach beginners to pull with the back for rows and deadlifts.
The centre line of the physique is built by compounds; the sides (arms, delts) are built by isolation, so novices should do some upper-body isolation.
The lower body can be built mostly with compounds; he built his legs without ever doing leg curls or leg extensions.
Without upper-body isolation novices end up with a massive torso, spaghetti arms and an incomplete back and shoulders.
Pull-ups and chin-ups aren't just a vertical pull, they are THE vertical pull; pulldowns are not an equivalent substitute.
He was an excellent calisthenics athlete, gave up pull-ups for almost two years when he got heavy, and when he returned could barely do five; he regrets the lost back development.
He dislikes 3x5 and 5x5 schemes: too little volume and too rigid; you're either shortchanging yourself or overexerting and then failing the next session.
Most novice programs have failure in mind: rather than an evolving rep range that pre-empts plateaus, they rush you into the wall as fast as possible and leave you there.
A program that adds 150 lbs to your deadlift but leaves you adding only 20 lbs over the next three years was a bad program.
Benching 3x5 every other day gives at most about 30 challenging horizontal press reps a week, not enough; there should be push-ups or dips added.
Novices don't need much volume but they need an introduction to volume.
Romanian deadlifts at 3x8 once or twice a week give about 24 challenging hip-hinge reps a week, not full ROM: not enough.
2x10 bicep curls (20 reps) is not enough volume.

Novices can ride strength gains for a long time because the brain adapts to the lift quickly; staying at fixed volume while load rises builds strength but less hypertrophy than adding volume as strength rises.
Programs that go pure strength and then dump you into high volume leave no bridge; novices should do both strength and volume in moderation.
Novices should be given rep range choices rather than fixed numbers, because they'll eventually have to build their own programs and need to learn early.
A good novice program isn't afraid of monotony: repeat the basics and some variations; landmine presses and fancy lifts come later, after mastering the basics.
Avoid extremes: don't get stuck in the mentality of only barbell movements or only the big three; do what works, not ideology.
Fierce 5 lacks hamstring work; squats and front squats emphasise quads and glutes, and you should do more hamstring work than quad work for knee health.
Vertical pulls are more critical than horizontal pulls for beginners.
Beginners don't need side raises; overhead press plus face pulls covers the shoulders.
Trap isolation can wait like calves because traps respond so well to isolation later; but heavy deadlifts are needed for trap growth early.
Forearms won't grow enough from pulls and rows; novices need hammer curls and some wrist flexion work.
Beginners are uncomfortable doing low-rep skull crushers, so do them light with more volume to make up the tonnage.
Training at home without a barbell, he built his lower back with bed bridges stacking plates on his belly for minutes at a time, and has never had a lower back injury.

A strong lower back prevents injuries for your whole career; back hyperextensions are the best lower back isolation because they teach pulling with the posterior chain (hamstrings, glutes) with the lower back as a rigid link.
Ab isolation is shunned because people think compounds suffice, but the deadlift, one of the best core compounds, isn't even in Fierce 5.
Two knee-flexion lifts are enough quad work for novices; neck, calves and traps can be worked later once you have a solid physique.
Novices should warm up with as many sets as they need (three or five) and never jump straight into heavy weight; static stretching is not a must.
Adding 10 lbs a week to lower body lifts and 5 lbs to upper body lifts is a good novice progression, and allowing extra reps when weight can't be added is good.

numbers.load: +10 lbs lower / +5 lbs upper per week

claims.claim: Fast linear progression leads full speed into a plateau, after which you either stagnate discouragingly or must deload and relearn training with volume and tonnage.

His modified Fierce 5: main lifts in rotating rep ranges (3 sets of 4-8, 6-10 or 8-12, extra sets if needed), deadlift and back squat variation on day B, cable rows, chin-ups, pull-ups and push-ups AMRAP, hyperextensions 4x15, skull crushers 4x10, curls 4x10, all as supersets.
He won't review 5/3/1 or the Cube method because they've been reviewed by hundreds; he prefers niche programs or viewers' own programs.
